title: Answer to Question: On the Reality of the Coup in Guinea
text:
Answer to Question: On the Reality of the Coup in Guinea

Question:

On 23/12/2008 it was announced in Conakry, the capital of Guinea, that military units had rebelled, and that was four hours after the announcement of the death of the president of the Guinean republic, General Lansana Conté. On the following day, the coup leaders announced the formation of a consultative council under the name "the National Council for Development and Democracy". And the appointment was announced of the soldier who had broadcast the coup leaders' statement on the first day by way of the country's official radio, namely Captain Moussa Camara, as head of this council. The prime minister opposed the coup at its beginning, and the commander of the armed forces supported the prime minister and called on the coup leaders to be loyal to the government... But the prime minister then went back and surrendered to the coup leaders after less than three days!

So what is the reality of the matter? Is what happened a local matter in which the coup leaders exploited the death of the president of the republic, or is it a regional or international event?

Answer:

Following what took place, and likewise the international positions that were declared towards the coup, all of it shows that the international struggle over Africa is not far from the events of the coup. To clarify that, we mention the following:

1- The head of the coup, Captain Moussa Camara, announced in the name of the coup leaders that they "do not intend to continue in power for more than two years, until presidential elections are held at the end of 2010" (BBC 24/12/2008). He also mentioned that the reasons necessitating the coup were, as he said: "The institutions of the republic have shown their inability to confront the crisis existing in the country, and from today the work of the constitution will be suspended and political and trade union activities will be suspended." And he added: "The country is living in a state of deep despair, and something had to be done to stop corruption and improve the economy" (BBC 24/12/2008). This indicates that the coup had been planned beforehand, and was not the product of the four hours after the death of the president, nor was it a reaction to the death of the country's president, especially as this captain who led the latest rebellion has led more than one rebellion, the last of which was in May of this year.

2- As for the international reactions, they came first from France, which is considered the holder of influence in Guinea, its former colony: "France said it would resist any coup attempt" (BBC 23/12/2008). And the spokesman for the foreign ministry, Eric Chevallier, said at a press conference: "We will not accept any situation that does not respect the constitution." And he added: "It appears that the legitimate authorities are in control of the situation in the country at present; we have a claim, and it seems the facts do not support it" (Al Jazeera 23/12/2008). It appears from these statements that France is fearful of the success of the coup leaders and rejects their movement, and it said that it would resist it! The French newspapers attacked the coup leaders and continued their criticisms of them; indeed some of them mocked them, as Le Figaro did when it said: "The Guinean soldiers roaming the city of Conakry have placed at the head of their country an obscure major who was head of the fuel department"!

3- As for the United States of America, the White House spokesman Tony Fratto announced: "We are working with our partners in the region and other countries and the African Union in order to encourage the institutions in Guinea to take all the necessary steps to establish a peaceful and democratic transfer of power in Guinea." And he added: "It is clear that the region is turbulent, and its history has mostly not seen this kind of peaceful and democratic transfer of power" (Al Jazeera 23/12/2004). This indicates that the United States' saying that it is in favour of a peaceful and democratic transfer of power is a false saying for democratic consumption, because it says at the same time that the region does not know the transfer of power by the peaceful and democratic method! So it leaves, then, nothing but the path of military coups, which the United States has so often applied in bringing its agents to power...!

The statement also indicates that America is satisfied with what took place and supports it implicitly. But it cannot support the coup leaders openly because of its mouthing of democracy and peaceful means, and it is known that these matters have no value for it except if they achieve its interests for it.

America's satisfaction with the coup and its implicit support for it is confirmed by what the spokesman for the American State Department, Robert Wood, declared. He told the American radio station "Sawa" "that the United States wants Guinea to return immediately to civilian democratic rule. And he said that Washington is displeased with the absence of a civilian element in the process of transferring power in Guinea at this stage. And he said that the United States has not yet taken a decision regarding the coup in Guinea, and it is consulting with its allies in an effort to take a coordinated position" (Al-Moheet page 25/12/2008). The words of this American official spokesman indicate that America is not against the coup, and implicitly supports it, because he said that America is displeased with the absence of a civilian element in the process of transferring power, and he did not say that it is displeased with the coup. Also, his saying that his country has not yet taken a decision means its approval of the coup, but it is waiting for the appropriate time for the explicit announcement of that. Had the coup not been in its interest, it would have raised the world against the coup leaders and not let it rest, as it does with many coups that do not suit its interests. Added to this is that the United States has requested the holding of elections in May next (Al Jazeera 26/12/2008), and this shows the implicit American support for the coup.

4- As for Britain, the commentary of the BBC on 24/12/2008, while reporting the news, said: "The division (in the Guinean army) may have dire consequences in view of the ethnic divisions in the army and in the country." The BBC added: "The divisions will affect the neighbouring countries of Sierra Leone, Liberia and Ivory Coast." And it also added: "Observers also stress that there are fears that these developments in Guinea will affect the situation in West Africa, where neighbouring countries such as Liberia, Sierra Leone and Ivory Coast have recently enjoyed relative stability after years of conflict." And it took a jab at the head of the coup, reporting that his comrades said of him "that he was not a brilliant student". This indicates that the English are not satisfied with the coup, and that they realise that the coup is not in their interest, and that a change will happen in the region, and that this change is not in favour of European influence; otherwise they would not have said that the coup has dire consequences and that it will affect the neighbouring countries...

5- Late on the night of Wednesday 24/12/2008, the leader of the rebels, Moussa Camara, declared himself president of the country, saying: "I am convinced, and I want to affirm that I am the president of the republic and the leader of the National Council for Democracy and Development." The prime minister, Ahmed Tidiane Souaré, responded to him with a statement to Radio France Internationale, saying that his government still exists and will remain so during the transitional period (Al Jazeera 25/12/2008). The same source mentioned that the chief of staff of the armed forces, Diarra Camara, sought to hold dialogue with the rebels to persuade them to adhere to the constitutional rules, which stipulate that the president of the National Assembly (parliament) becomes interim president of the country. This indicates that there are two different or contending parties: one of them made up of military men led by Moussa Camara, and the other led by the head of the armed forces, and with him the government and parliament. The leader of the coup leaders hastened to declare himself president of the republic in order to consolidate his authority and to prevent anyone else from declaring himself president of the republic, such as the head of the armed forces for example, and to prevent the appointment of the president of parliament as interim president. It is worth mentioning that the deceased president Lansana Conté seized power by a military coup in 1984, one week after the death of the former president Ahmed Sékou Touré.

6- From all of the above it becomes clear:

That what happened falls within an international struggle, between America on the one hand and Europe, "France and Britain", and especially France, on the other hand; and that the United States is behind the coup leaders and supports them; and that France and Britain are against the coup, and that their influence in West Africa will be threatened if America succeeds in Guinea-Conakry.

7- This is concerning what happened falling within the circle of the international struggle.

As for the prime minister's surrender to the head of the coup leaders after he had been against him, the reality of the matter is as follows:

A- Yes, the prime minister Ahmed Tidiane Souaré, and with him 30 ministers, surrendered to the coup leaders, and he declared his loyalty to their leader, saying to him: "We thank you and place ourselves at your disposal" (Al Jazeera 26/12/2008). And he praised him, describing him as wise (the American CNN 26/12/2008). The prime minister Ahmed Souaré had opposed the coup leaders at the beginning. The commander of the armed forces, Diarra Camara, had supported the prime minister and considered him the one who represents the country at present, and was demanding that the rebels surrender. The fact that the prime minister surrendered indicates that the coup leaders have succeeded in taking hold of the reins of affairs.

B- This is from one aspect. From another aspect, it indicates that France and Britain realised that the coup had succeeded or almost so, and that opposing it would be of no use, and that they preferred to accept the crumbs from America in return for instructing the prime minister and the army commander to surrender to the coup leaders. It is as if France and Britain obtained from America the preservation of some of their interests in Guinea, with America's interests remaining in the forefront in that country, and so the surrender took place.

8- It is known that Bush, in his last visit in February of this year, visited five countries in Africa, some of them in West Africa, which indicates that America gives priority to West Africa in an attempt to extend its influence over all the countries of Africa, from its west to its east and from its north to its south. We recall Bush's statement before he set off there, when he said: "Africa is of the utmost importance to the American strategy, and the African situation has a direct effect on American security itself" (the Chinese People's Daily newspaper on 25/2/2008). So he made Africa a decisive issue for the United States, as he mentioned that it affects America's security directly! It is as if he wants to make the south-eastern shore of the Atlantic, that is, West Africa, and what lies beyond it towards the east, an internal American matter specific to America, along the lines of the Monroe Doctrine, which made the western shore of the Atlantic a decisive issue for the United States, such that any encroachment upon it is a direct encroachment upon the United States. And this position of Bush is like the position of Monroe against his allies, the enemies, the European colonialists.

The wealth of Africa is enormous, and part of it is oil, as it has large oil reserves at which the mouth of the big brother of the Western colonialists waters! It came in the report of Al-Ahram International on 16/6/2007 that the American National Communications Council expects that the coast of Guinea will supply the United States with about 24-25% of its total oil imports by the year 2020. The African International Policy Center also expects that the oil profits of the coast of Guinea will reach a trillion dollars by 2020 if the price of a barrel remains above 50 dollars. Guinea is the largest exporter in the world of the raw material "bauxite", from which aluminium is made, and its location on the Atlantic Ocean is strategic, so that the transport of energy from there to America would be faster and safer, more secure than from the Middle East region, which is threatened with falling into the hands of its Muslim people out of the hand of America and the colonialist West; and at a cheap cost, since the distance is considered relatively close to America. It is a candidate for transporting the oil of many African countries in the future from its gulf, if America controls the region.
